facts.text: On this date in 1793, the Louvre opened as a public museum — converting a royal palace that had housed French kings for centuries into a space any citizen could enter, a genuinely radical act at the time.
On August 10, 1628, the Swedish warship Vasa sank 1,300 meters into her maiden voyage. She was so top-heavy she capsized in a light breeze, taking 30 lives and Sweden's naval pride with her.
Mongolia has more horses than people — roughly 4.3 million horses to 3.4 million humans — and a third of the population still lives nomadically, moving with their herds across the steppe.

The Philippines is the world's largest supplier of nurses, with over 25% of all internationally deployed nurses being Filipino — a deliberate postcolonial export strategy built into the national education system.

Istanbul is the only city that spans two continents, but its European side holds just 3% of the land while housing over a third of its 16 million people — making it one of the densest urban corridors on Earth.

On August 10, 1792, the French monarchy effectively ended when the Tuileries Palace fell — the Paris Bourse, founded just four years earlier, suspended trading that day and wouldn't fully reopen for years.

On August 10, 1949, Congress signed the National Security Act amendments creating the Department of Defense — Lockheed's stock had already quietly doubled in the prior 18 months anticipating the Cold War buildup.
The S&P 500 has closed higher on the Friday before August options expiration more than 70% of the time since 2000, a quirk traders call 'pinning' as market makers defend strike prices.
Berkshire Hathaway's Class A shares have never split. At over $700,000 each, a single share costs more than the median American house.
The Dutch tulip mania of 1637 peaked not with rare bulbs but with futures contracts — paper promises on tulips not yet planted, making it history's first recorded derivatives bubble.
On this date in 1990, the Magellan spacecraft entered Venus's orbit — a planet where a day lasts longer than its year.
Your skeleton is not static. Every decade, you replace roughly 100% of your bone mass, atom by atom.
On this date in 1675, King Charles II ordered the Royal Observatory founded — the original prime meridian was drawn through a building that no longer stands.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
Octopuses have three hearts, blue blood, and neurons distributed throughout their arms — each limb can taste, touch, and make decisions independently.
On this day in 1628, the Swedish warship Vasa sank 20 minutes into her maiden voyage. She was raised intact in 1961 — the sailors' lunches were still on the tables.
Missouri entered the Union on August 10, 1821. It is older than the photograph, the postage stamp, and the word 'scientist.'
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. The pyramids were already ancient history to her.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — 21 years before the American Civil War ended, and a full 33 years before Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone.
Oxford University was teaching students before the Aztec Empire existed. When Montezuma was born, Oxford had already been running for 300 years.

Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. It felt inevitable the moment it existed.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home that may never have existed. Untranslatable, it folds homesickness, grief, and nostalgia into a single breath.
On this day in 1519, Magellan's fleet departed Seville — giving the world 'circumnavigate,' from Latin circum (around) + navigare (to sail). The word outlasted every sailor on that voyage.

Petrichor (n.): the smell of rain on dry earth. Named in 1964 by Australian scientists Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas, from Greek petra (stone) + ichor, the fluid said to flow in the veins of gods.
On this day in 1675, the Royal Observatory at Greenwich was founded — anchoring the word 'meridian' to a single iron line, from Latin meridianus: of midday, the moment the sun crosses due south.
